J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The appellant, a distribution licensee in the State of Telangana, is
aggrieved by the order dated 04.08.2025 passed by the 2nd respondent
Telangana Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the
Commission”) whereby the Commission has allowed the appellant’s petition
bearing O.P. No.21/2024 (old No. O.P. 116/2022) under Section 86(1)(b) of
the Electricity Act, 2003 and accorded approval to the Power Purchase
Agreement (PPA) dated 10.10.2022 executed between appellant and the 1st
respondent despite the fact that the appellant had sought withdrawal of the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 2 of 30

petition vide letter dated 03.10.2023 addressed in this regard to the
Commission.
2. The 1st respondent M/s Hyderabad MSW Energy Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is
a generating company engaged in Waste to Energy (WTE) projects and is
operating WTE power project located at Jawaharnagar, District Medchal,
Hyderabad. It had entered into a PPA dated 19.02.2020 with the appellant
for sale of power from its said 19.8MW WTE power project at a tariff to be
determined by the Commission from time to time. Subsequently, the 1st
respondent requested for enhancement of the capacity of its power plant
from 19.8MW to 24MW capacity, which was acceded to by the appellant.
Accordingly, the PPA dated 19.02.2020 required to be amended and a draft
amended PPA dated 10.10.2022 was prepared.
3. The appellant then approached the Commission with petition bearing
OP No.116/2022 seeking approval of the Commission of the said draft
amended PPA dated 10.10.2022 under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity
Act, 2003. Before any order could be passed on the said petition, the
appellant addressed a letter dated 03.10.2023 to the Commission requesting
permission to withdraw the petition on the ground that there had been no
augmentation of any equipment of the power project, and therefore, the plant
will not be able to generate 24MW of power, however, vide order dated
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 3 of 30

30.10.2023, the Commission rejected the request of appellant to withdraw
the petition and also declined to give consent to the amended PPA dated
10.10.2022.
4. The 1st Respondent assailed the said order dated 30th October, 2023
of the Commission before this Tribunal in Appeal No. 63 of 2024 which came
to be allowed by this Tribunal thereby remanding the matter to the
Commission for passing fresh order in accordance with the law upon
affording reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, particularly
the 1st Respondent.
5. The Commission then restored the petition No. 116 of 2022 and re-
numbered it as O.P. No. 21 of 2024. It appears that during the further
proceedings of the petition, the Commission felt it pertinent to appoint a
Committee of experts on the following terms of reference :-
"The main objective is to inspect the equipment of the generator
i.e, 19.8 MW Waste to Energy Power Plant of M/s. Hyderabad
MSWESPL, at Jawahar Nagar, Kapra Mandal of Medchal -
Malkjagiri District, Hyderabad to report as to whether the existing
equipment of the generator is capable of generating and injecting
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 4 of 30

24 MW of power, as mentioned in the amended Power Purchase Agreement
entered by the said firm with TGSPDCL.".
6. As noted in the impugned order, the Expert Committee inspected the
power project on 21st February, 2025 and made its conclusions and
recommendations as under :-
"3. Based on the above observations, the committee is of the
view that the existing WTE plant of M/s HMSWESPL is able to
generate 24 MW power periodically as demonstrated during the
visit of the committee and shown in the selected generation data
provided by HMSWESPL. However, a continuous demonstration
of 24 MW generation cannot be ascertained based on the data
provided. It is recommended that the TGERC may approach
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) for appropriate
guidelines for performance acceptance test of MSW/RDF-based
Waste to Energy Plants based on continuous run without LDO
support for a minimum duration. TGERC, based on the MNRE
guidelines, may seek a performance acceptance test for the
plant to demonstrate a continuous capacity of 24 MW".
7. Both the Appellant and the 1st Respondent filed their objections to the
report of the Expert Committee which have been duly considered by the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 5 of 30

Commission. Following points were formulated by the Commission for its
considerations in the petition :-
"1. Whether the existing equipment of the M/s. HMESPL
plant is capable of generating 24 MW power.
2. And if so, whether the request of the TGSPDCL to accord
consent for amendment of PPA of 10.10.2022 can be acceded
even after TGSPDCL sought to withdraw the petition."
8. Both the points have been decided by the Commission in favour of the
1st Respondent in the impugned order. The final order passed by the
Commission is as under :-
I. The petition filed by TGSPDCL seeking to give the consent
to the draft first amendment dated 10.10.2022 to the original
PPA dated 19.02.2020 in respect of enhancing of waste to
energy plant from 19.8 MW to 24 MW capacity situated at
Jawaharnagar, Kapra Mandal, Medchal - Malkajgiri district
is allowed.
II. Consequently, the prayer of the TGSPDCL made in the
letter dated 03.10.2023 seeking to withdraw the petition is
hereby dismissed.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 6 of 30

III. The TGSPDCL is directed to submit amended PPA before
this Commission within one month from the date of receipt of
this letter.
9. We have heard Mr. D. Abhinav Rao, Learned Counsel for the
Appellant, Mr. Sanjay Sen, Learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of
Respondent No. 1 and Mr. Rajat Srivastava, learned Counsel for
Respondent No. 2.
10. Learned Counsel for the Appellant argued that the impugned order of
the Commission disallowing the request of the Appellant to withdraw O.P No.
21 of 2024 is in the teeth of Order 23 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure
(CPC), 1908. He would submit that a petitioner has a right to withdraw its
petition at any stage and neither the Commission nor the Respondent can
raise objections to such prayer of the petitioner. He cited the judgment of
Hon'ble Supreme Court of Anil Kumar Singh Vs. Vijay Pal Singh and Ors.
(2018) 12 SCC 584 in support of his submissions. He would further argue
that recognition of capacity of power plant as 24 MW without physical
augmentation and production is erroneous for the reason that the Expert
Committee also, in its report, had stated that the plant is unable to generate
24 MW power continuously. He submitted that admittedly, the existing 19.8
MW power plant has not been augmented with any further equipment which
is a sine qua non for any valid capacity enhancement, consistent with
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 7 of 30

industry practice, as well as regulatory norms and, therefore, the impugned
order of the Commission granting approval of the amended PPA dated 10th
October, 2022 suffers from serious infirmities.
11. Learned Counsel also submitted that the Commission vide tariff order
dated 18th April, 2020 has determined the fixed charges as well as variable
charges payable to a power generator by assuming certain operational
parameters and accordingly, alteration of any such parameter such as
capacity enhancement without any additional expenditure, calls for re-
determination of tariff. In other words, according to the Learned Counsel
since the capacity enhancement is resulting in improving the PLF, the same
needs to be factored in the tariff with suitable reduction. He submitted that
the tariff payable to the Respondent No. 1 should be re-visited by the
Commission with revised operation parameters.
12. On behalf of the 1st Respondent, it was argued by the Learned Senior
Counsel that once a PPA was executed between the parties with their
consent and was also acted upon by supply of power from the power project
of 1st Respondent to the Appellant in terms thereof which is evident from the
joint meter readings, there was no occasion for the Appellant to seek
withdrawal of the petition before the Commission. He would further submit
that the regulation of a power procurement by a Distribution Licensee i.e. an
approval/or determination of the procurement terms/tariff is solely within the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 8 of 30

domain of the Commission and not a matter be left to unilateral choice of a
party to a PPA. He also pointed out that the Appellant actively participated in
the process of appointment of the Expert Committee and even nominated its
members. He submitted that the report of the Committee makes it clear that
concerns of Appellant for augmentation were fully addressed by the
Committee.
13. Learned Senior Counsel also pointed out that the letter dated 16th
October, 2023 addressed by the Appellant to the Commission seeking
withdrawal of the petition was after the arguments were concluded in the
petition and order was reserved on 21st September, 2023. He would argue
that once hearing is completed in a quasi judicial proceedings and order is
reserved, the pronouncement of order cannot be sought to be aborted by
addressing a communication to the Secretary of the Commission as there is
no hiatus between the date of reserving of the order and date of pronouncing
of the judgement. According to the Learned Senior Counsel such course of
action is unknown to law and undermines the regulatory process.
14. To buttress his submission, Learned Senior Counsel cited a judgement
of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Andhra Pradesh Southern Power
Distribution Power Co. Ltd. Vs. Hinduja National Power Corpn. Ltd., (2022)
5 SCC 484. He also relied upon the previous judgement of this Tribunal in
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 9 of 30

Hinduja National Power Corporation Ltd. Vs. Andhra Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission and Ors. 2020, SCC online APTEL 3 wherein it is
held that the proceedings before the State Regulatory Commission are not
in the nature of a lis, as in case of civil suit before a Civil Court.
15. On these submissions, Learned Senior Counsel urged us to dismiss
the appeal.
Our Analysis :-
16. The draft PPA incorporating the enhanced capacity of the power
project of the 1st Respondent as 24 MW was entered into between the
parties on 10th October, 2022. This was done in pursuance to the accent
accorded by the Appellant to the augmentation of the existing capacity of the
power project from 19.8 to 24 MW conveyed vide letter dated 16th March,
2022. Subsequently, the Appellant filed a petition under 86(1)(b) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 before the Commission seeking approval of the said
amended PPA dated 10th October, 2022.
17. It appears that the petition came up for hearing before the Commission
on 1st September, 2023 on which date the Appellant for the first time
submitted to the Commission that the amended PPA has been entered into
without verifying the technical parameters for enhancing the capacity from
19.8 MW to 24 MW. When the Commission sought to examine the technical
aspect and required the petitioner to submit the details, two contradictory
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 10 of 30

reports were placed at the disposal of the Commission. Both the reports were
secured by the Appellant itself, one being from its internal officers and the
other from an external agency. The Commission expressed its displeasure
in the way the matter had been handled by the Appellant and sought to know
why these aspects have not been examined before filing the petition. The
officers of the Appellant present during the hearing replied that they had
relied upon the recommendations of Telangana State Renewable Energy
Development Corporation which has suggested the fuel and rating capacity
as well as the certification done by the Chief Electrical Inspector for the State
of Telangana who had certified about the rating capacity of the plant.
Recording all these contentions/submissions, the Commission reserved the
order on the petition. For the sake of reference, we hereby extract the said
order of the Commission dated 01.09.2023 hereinbelow :-

Petitioner(s) Respondent(s)

____________________________________________________________________________________

representative of the petitioner as well as officers accompany the

having perused the record took exception to the way the petition had
been filed without examining the requirement of information and the
necessity of providing complete comprehensive fair information in the
matter. The petitioner has into a draft amendment PPA without
verifying the technical parameters for enhancement of capacity from
19.8 MW to 24 MW. Moreover, when the Commission sought to
examine the technical aspects and required the petitioner to submit
the details, two contradictory reports have been placed at the disposal
of the Commission. Both the reports have been secured by the
petitioner itself, one being from its internal officers and the other from
the external agency. These reports relating to technical examination
should have been done at the first instance itself before filing the
petition. The petitioner should have examined the request of
enhanced capacity considering the technical parameters before
approaching the Commission for approval of draft amendment PPA.
The Commission sought to know from the officers of the petitioner as
to why the aspects have not been examined before filing of the
petition. The officers present have replied that they relied on the
recommendations of Telangana State Renewable Energy
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 12 of 30

Development Corporation, which had suggested the fuel and rating
capacity. Also, reliance was placed on the certification done by the
Chief Electrical Inspector for the State of Telangana, who had
certified about the rating capacity of the plant. They sought to explain
the said details. The Commission expressed displeasure in the way
the matter was handled and also sought to know how the petitioner is
injecting higher capacity of more than the rated capacity. There is no
reply from them, however, they tried to explain on these aspects only
after the Commission had raised the questions on the same.
At this stage, the representative of the petitioner sought some time to
rectify the defects and also place the appropriate material or else to
return the petition. However, the Commission pointed out that since
the matter has been called for hearing on the maintainability, it has
no other option except to decide the matter either to entertain or
refuse the same by rejecting it. Therefore, the Commission expressed
its views in the matter and would pass orders accordingly on it.

18. After the orders on the petition were reserved by the Commission as
stated hereinabove, a letter dated 3rd October, 2023 was sent by the
Appellant to the Secretary of the Commission with a permission to withdraw
the petition on the ground that amendment to the PPA for enhancement of
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 13 of 30

capacity was acceded to in expectation of the addition/augmentation of the
power project but site inspection report submitted by the team of engineers
of the Appellant shows that there is no change through
addition/augmentation in the rating of the generator and associate
equipments vis boiler, turbine, generator etc. at the plant and hence without
such addition/augmentation the proposed enhancement of capacity from
19.8 MW to 24 MW is not possible.
19. Issue which arises for our consideration in these facts and
circumstances of the case is whether a Distribution Licensee can be
permitted to withdraw the petition under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity
Act, 2003 seeking approval of the PPA executed by it with a power generator,
not on the ground that it does not require the power or that the tariff fixed in
the proposed PPA is on the higher side but on some other ground. The
answer to this issue would require us to discuss in detail the scope of Section
86(1)(b) of the Act as well as the powers of the Commission thereunder.
20. Section 86 of the Electricity Act, 2003 reads as under :-
"Section 86. (Functions of State Commission): --- (1) The State
Commission shall discharge the following functions, namely: -
(a) determine the tariff for generation, supply, transmission and wheeling of
electricity, wholesale, bulk or retail, as the case may be, within the State:
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 14 of 30

Provided that where open access has been permitted to a category of
consumers under section 42, the State Commission shall determine only the
wheeling charges and surcharge thereon, if any, for the said category of
consumers;
(b)"regulate electricity purchase and procurement process of distribution
licensees including the price at which electricity shall be procured from the
generating companies or licensees or from other sources through
agreements for purchase of power for distribution and supply within the
State;"
21. This Section confers power upon the State Electricity Commissions to
"regulate" the electricity purchase and procurement undertaken by the
distribution licensees for distribution and supply within the State, such
regulation covering various aspects including "the price at which electricity
shall be procured from the generation companies or the licensees or from
other sources". What the Commission is empowered to regulate in the
'electricity purchase' and 'procurement process' of a distribution licensee.
The purchase of electricity can be by way of an agreement with regards to
the source, quantum and price. However, the procurement process can be
either by way of bidding or by negotiations (which may involve an
agreement). In this regard, the following observations of the Hon'ble
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 15 of 30

Supreme Court in Tata Power Co. Ltd. Vs. Reliance Energy Ltd. (supra) are
apposite :-
"108. A generating company, if the liberalisation and privatisation policy
is to be given effect to, must be held to be free to enter into an
agreement and in particular long-term agreement with the distribution
agency; terms and conditions of such an agreement, however, are not
unregulated. Such an agreement is subject to grant of approval by the
Commission. The Commission has a duty to check if the allocation of
power is reasonable. If the terms and conditions relating to quantity,
price, mode of supply, the need of the distributing agency vis-à-vis the
consumer, keeping in view its long-term need are not found to be
reasonable, approval may not be granted.
109. A generating company has to make a huge investment and
assurances given to it that subject to the provisions of the Act it would
be free to generate electricity and supply the same to those who intend
to enter into an agreement with it. Only in terms of the said statutory
policy, it makes huge investment. If all its activities are subject to
regulatory regime, it may not be interested in making investment. The
business in regard to allocation of electricity at the hands of the
generating company was the subject-matter of the licensing regime.
While interpreting the statute it must be borne in mind that such a
mechanism should not come back.
110. That, however, would not mean that the generating company is
absolutely free from all regulations. Such regulations are permissible
under the 2003 Act; one of them being fair dealing with the distributor.
Thus, other types of regulations should not be brought in which were
not contemplated under the statutory scheme. If it is exercising its
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 16 of 30

dominant position, Section 60 would come into play. It is only in a situation
where a generator may abuse or misuse its position the Commission would
be entitled to issue a direction. The regulatory regime of the Commission,
thus, can be enforced against a generating company if the condition
precedent therefor becomes applicable."
22. Section 86(1)(b), thus, empowers the State Commission to oversee
the purchase and procurement of power by the distribution licensees. In
other words, the State Commission is entrusted with the power to regulate
the prices of sale and purchase of electricity between the generating
companies and distribution licensees through agreements known as Power
Purchase Agreements (PPAs) in order to ensure that such sale and
purchase of electricity is not against the interest of the consumers. The
Commission is vested with the jurisdiction to determine tariff at which a
distribution licensee should procure/purchase electricity, which it exercises
either by determining tariff under Section 62 of the Act or by adopting tariff
discovered through a competitive bidding process under Section 63 or by
issuing generic tariff orders.
23. Therefore, once a petition under Section 86(1)(b) of the electricity Act,
2003 filed before the Commission by Distribution Licensee seeking approval
of the PPA, the Commission only needs to ascertain the need of the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 17 of 30

Distribution Licensee to procure the power under the PPA and the
reasonableness of the price at which the power is sought to be procured
under the PPA. Once the Commission is satisfied that the Distribution
Licensee genuinely requires the power to be supplied to the consumers and
the tariff fixed under the PPA is not exorbitant or above the prevalent market
price of the power, it has no option except to accord its approval to the PPA.
However, it may suggest changes to any clause in the PPA which, it feels,
would be against the interest of the consumers.
24. In the instant case, the Appellant had not sought withdrawal of the
petition under Section 86(1)(b) on the ground that it does not require the
power from the power project of the 1st Respondent or, the tariff fixed in the
PPA has been counted to be exorbitantly high. The withdrawal of the petition
was sought on the ground that the power project would not be able to
generate 24 MW of power continuously in the absence of any
addition/augmentation in the rating of its main equipment i.e.
generator/turbine/boiler etc. In other words, the case of the Appellant seems
to be that the amended PPA dated 10th October, 2022 has been signed by
it on some mis-representation.
25. Considering the scope and ambit of regulatory powers conferred upon
the Electricity Regulatory Commission under Section 86(1)(b), we are of the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 18 of 30

opinion that mere misrepresentation alone would not entitle a distribution
licensee to seek withdrawal of the petition for approval of PPA from the
Commission. The discom must establish before the Commission that due to
the misrepresentation of facts there would be undue increase in tariff payable
by it to the power generator which would, in turn, adversely affect the
interests of the end consumers of the electricity. Any purported
misrepresentation without impacting the tariff prejudicially qua the discom
would be insignificant and thus irrelevant for considering whether or not to
approve the PPA.
26. A PPA is like any other commercial contract executed between the two
parties. The only distinction between the two is that a PPA becomes effective
and implementable only upon getting approval from the appropriate
regulatory commission under Section 86(1)(b) whereas the normal
commercial contracts become effective from the date of their execution.
Therefore, in case a party to the PPA feels that he executed the same on
account of some misrepresentation on the part of other party to the
agreement, he has the option to rescind from the agreement which can be
done even after the PPA is approved by the appropriate Commission. While
deciding a petition under Section 86(1)(b), the Commission does not act as
a civil court deciding a lis between the parties. Accordingly, the Commission
only satisfies itself only about (i) requirement of the discom of the power
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 19 of 30

under the PPA; (ii) reasonableness of the tariff fixed in the PPA; and (iii)
compliance of the relevant provisions of the Electricity Act as well as the
rules/regulations framed thereunder, before according approval to a PPA.
For seeking recession of the PPA on the ground of fraud, misrepresentation,
undue influence etc., the affected party shall have to initiate appropriate civil
action which may be either a petition under Section 86(1) (f) of the Act (in
case it impacts the tariff) or a civil suit before a civil court (in case it does not
impact the tariff).
27. In the instant case, the Appellant has concededly not elected to rescind
the PPA as it has neither served any notice in this regard upon the 1st
Respondent nor has initiated any legal proceedings. So, once the Appellant
has elected to proceed further with the PPA notwithstanding the
misrepresentation, its request seeking withdrawal of the petition under
Section 86(1)(b) was not maintainable at all.
28. Now let us proceed to determine whether, in fact, there had been any
misrepresentation held out by the 1st Respondent to the Appellant. Section
18 of the Contract Act, 1872 defines "Misrepresentation" as false or
misleading statements that induces a party to enter into a contract without
any fraudulent intent to deceive. We quote Section 18 hereunder :-
"18. "Misrepresentation" defined.-"Misrepresentation" means and
includes-
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 20 of 30

(I) the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the
information of the person making it, of that which is not true,
though he believes it to be true;
(II) any breach of duty which, without an intent to deceive, gains
an advantage to the person committing it, or any one claiming
under him; by misleading another to his prejudice, or to the
prejudice of any one claiming under him;
(III) causing, however innocently, a party to an agreement, to make
a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject
of the agreement."
29. Thus, if one party to the contract induces the other to enter into the
contract by misrepresenting, though innocently, any material fact specially
within his own knowledge, the party misled can avoid the contract. However,
it is not each and every misrepresentation which would render a contract to
be avoided. It is only where the facts are specially within one party's
knowledge, a positive duty of disclosure is obvious and the contract would
be avoidable by mere passive failure to communicate that material fact.
However, there is no positive duty of disclosure between the contracting
parties where the facts are not by their very nature more accessible to one
than to the other, though one party may have a specific informative which he
knows that the other has not. Mere silence is no misrepresentation when the
other party has the occasion and means to know the fact before entering into
the contract. Thus the contract is not voidable if the party who suffered the
mis-representation had the means to discover the truth with ordinary
diligence.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 21 of 30

vide Ref 3rd Cited above (Copy enclosed as Annex-II). M/s. TSPCB
has accorded Consent for Establishment of our existing capacity
from 19.8 MW to 48 MW vide Ref 4th Cited above (Copy enclosed
as Annex-III) and M/s. TSPCB accorded amendment of Consent for
Operation from 19.8 MW to 24 MW vide Ref 5th Cited above (Copy
enclosed as Annex-IV).
Further, M/S. TSREDCO has provided Proceedings and executed

MW to 48 MW in Phased manner. Accordingly, the said expansion
is being carried out as under in the same premises to achieve the
capacity from the existing 19.8 MW to 48 MW as per aforementioned
proceedings.
a) Phase-1: Augmentation of the present operating capacity of
19.8 MW to 24 MW
b) Phase-2: To set up, a New 24 MW RDF based WTE plant
We are herewith enclosing the following documents for your ready
reference.

Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 23 of 30

31. Perusal of these contents of the letter would reveal that the 1st
Respondent has nowhere stated that any addition/augmentation in the rating
of the generator and its associate equipments namely boiler, turbine etc. has
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 24 of 30

been done by it. The letter merely says that the operating capacity is being
expanded and enhanced from 19.8 MW to 24 MW. It was for the Appellant
to inspect the power project to ascertain whether any addition/augmentation
in the rating of the generator and its associate equipments has been carried
out. The Appellant had the opportunity and means to discover the actual
changes, if any, carried out by the 1st Respondent in the power station for
enhancement of its capacity. Such exercise ought to have been done prior
to signing the amended PPA dated 10.10.2022 or at least prior to filing the
petition under Section 86(1)(b), as was done by it after the filing of the
petition. on the basis of which letter dated 03.10.2023 was addressed by it
to the Commission seeking withdrawal of the petition. Once the Appellant
chose not to make any endeavour to discover the actual facts despite having
opportunity and means to do so and signed the amendment to the PPA an
also filed petition under Section 86(1)(b) for its approval, it cannot be hear
now to say that the amended PPA was executed by it on mis-representation.
32. Thus, it is limpid from the facts and circumstances of this case that the
2nd Respondent had not held out any false representation of any kind to the
Appellant and, therefore, the contention of the Appellant that the amend PPA
dated 10th October, 2022 was executed by it due to mis-representation is
without any basis.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 25 of 30

33. The contention of the Appellant that the power project of the Appellant
would not be able to generate 24 MW of power in the absence of any
addition/augmentation in the rating of the main equipment i.e.
generator/turbine/boiler etc. has been rightly repelled by the Commission in
the impugned order.
34. As we have already noted hereinabove that during the proceedings of
the petition, the Commission constituted an expert committee comprising of
Prof. Anoop Singh, IIT Kanpur, Prof. SK. Singh, Vice Chancellor, Rajasthan
Technical University and Mr. Asif Iqbal, Deputy Director, CEA to report as to
whether the existing equipment of the generator of the 2nd Respondent is
capable of generating and injecting 24 MW of power. It appears that the
Committee visited the power plant of 2nd Respondent on 21st February,
2025 and permitted the representative of both sides to submit data and to
make presentations. In its report submitted to the Commission on 20th
March, 2025, the expert Committee stated that based on the observations,
the Committee is of the view that the existing WTE plant of 2nd Respondent
is able to generate 24 MW power periodically as demonstrated during the
visit of the Committee and shown in the selected generation data provided
by 2nd Respondent. The Committee also added in its report that continuous
demonstration of 24 MW generation cannot be ascertained on the basis of
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 26 of 30

data provided to it and recommended a performance acceptance test for the
plant for such demonstration.
35. Along with the report, the Expert Committee also enclosed a letter
dated 26th February, 2025 addressed by M/s. TD Power Systems Limited
(Upon which the 2nd Respondent had placed order for supply, installation
and commissioning of 19.8 MW alternator for the power plant through M/s.
Greenesol Power Systems Private Ltd.), in which it is stated that standard
TC-210 frame size alternator has been supplied to the 2nd Respondent
which supports the capacity range from 18 MW to 24 MW. The letter further
mentions that although the name plate reflects buyer's specified quantity of
19.8 MW, TC-210 alternator is engineered to operate continuously up to 24
MW. The original manufacturer of the alternator has also endorsed in the
said letter that the machine installed by them is capable of producing 24 MW
of power continuously.
36. On the basis of contents of the said letter, the Commission has
observed in paragraph No. 23 of the impugned order as under :-
"23. This Commission, having perused the letter issued by the Original
Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) dated 26.02.2025, finds no merit in
relying solely upon the nameplate inscriptions of the generator to
delineate its operational capacity. It is trite law that mere form cannot
triumph over substance, and technical inscriptions are not watertight
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 27 of 30

indicators of capacity of the plant. The capacity of the plant to generate
power depends upon frame size of alternator, other connected
equipment and relative factors. Hence, the Commission is persuaded
that the plant's capacity is not circumscribed by the superficial label
affixed thereto, but by the embedded design margin envisaged ab initio.
Therefore, the argument of the TGSPDCL that since the name plate
inscriptions shows only 19.8 MW of power, it cannot generate 24 MW
of power cannot be accepted."
37. We are unable to find any flaw or infirmity in these observations of the
Commission. Once the original manufacturer of the machine endorses that the
machine installed in the power station of the 2nd Respondent is capable of
producing of 24 MW of power continuously and the machine actually was able
to generate 24 MW of power during the visit of the Expert Committee, there
does not remain any doubt that the generator installed by the 2nd Respondent
would not be able to generate 24 MW of power in the absence of any
additional/augmentation as contended by the Appellant. The Commission has
correctly observed in the impugned order that there exists neither any statutory
mandate nor jurisprudential precedent requiring the physical
addition/augmentation for such enhancement. When the generator in question
had been originally designed to produce 24 MW of power as certified by its
manufacturer, there was no need for any further addition/augmentation to it for
enhancement of its capacity from 19.8 MW to 24 MW.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 28 of 30

38. It is true that, as noted herein above, as per the report of the Expert
Committee, the continuous demonstration of 24 MW generation of power could not
be ascertained on the basis of the data provided to it. On this aspect, Commission
has correctly observed that there are no guidelines, regulations rules framed either
by the Commission itself or by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission or by
Ministry of Renewable Energy, Govt. of India mandating period of continuous
generation of specific MW of power to determine the capacity of renewable energy
power plant. The Commission has noted that in case of thermal power projects as
per the CERC Regulations, the thermal power plant has run continuously for 72
hours in order to determine that thermal plant is capable of generating specific
Megawatts of power and in case of power being generated through non-
conventional renewable energy sources like wind, solar, MSW and biomass etc.,
it is not possible for a plant to generate specific megawatt continuously, as it
depends upon many relative factors including weather, nature of fuel, moisture
content etc.
39. In this regard, it is also to be noted that the Appellant has given the
"Certificate of Contracted Capacity" to the 2nd Respondent in achieving 19.8 MW
of power at 16:00 hours on 11.12.2020 and at that time the Appellant did not ask
the generator to demonstrate continuous generation of 19.8 MW of power as the
condition precedent prior to issuing the said Certificate. Therefore, insistence on
the part of the Appellant in demanding the 2nd Respondent to continuous
generation of 24 MW of power in order to enhance the 19.8 MW to 24 MW is not
justified.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.302 of 2025 Page 29 of 30

40. We may also note that the power project in question is a Waste to
Energy (WTE) project converting the garbage into electrical energy. By doing
so, the power project is not only useful in disposing of large amounts of the
garbage and, therefore, is in public interest but also adds to the power
generation thereby reducing the scarcity of power in the State of Telangana.
Such type of power projects need to be encouraged. The enhancement of
the capacity of the Appellant's power project from 19.8 MW to 24 MW would
mean that it will utilize more garbage and would produce more power.
Therefore, permitting the Appellant to withdraw the petition filed by it under
Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act or refusal on the part of the Commission
to approve the amended PPA date 10.10.2022 executed between the parties
would be doing a great dis-service to the nation at large and thus not
advisable.
Conclusion
41. Bearing in mind the above discussion, we do not find any error or
infirmity in the impugned order of the Commission. The appeal is sans any
merit and dismissed as such. All Pending IAs also stand disposed of.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 30th day of October, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present Appeal has been preferred by M/s Bhoruka Power Corporation
Limited challenging the Order dated 18.12.2015 passed by the Haryana
Electricity Regulatory Commission (“HERC” or “Commission”) in Case No.
HERC/PRO-59 of 2014, whereby the Appellant’s petition seeking re-
determination of tariff in respect of its 6 MW Small Hydel Power Project at
Dadupur, Yamuna Nagar, Haryana (“Project”) due to non-availability of Full
Supply Level (FSL in short) of 916 ft, came to be rejected.
Page 2 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
Description of Parties:-
2. The Appellant - M/s Bhoruka Power Corporation Limited (“BPCL”) is a
Generating company in terms of Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act and has set
up a 4x1.5 MW Small Hydro Power Plant in Yamuna Nagar District of Haryana in
the year 2010 ("Project").
3. The Respondent No. 1- The Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission is
the State Regulatory Commission for the state of Haryana and exercising
powers vested under Section 86 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
4. The Respondent No. 2-Haryana Power Purchase Centre ("HPPC) is a joint
forum of Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (“UHBVNL”) and Dakshin
Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (“DHBVNL”) for procurement of power on
behalf of the these State Distribution Licensees.
5. The Respondent No. 3, is the Irrigation Department, Government of
Haryana, the department of State Government responsible for the administration
and management of irrigation works in the State of Haryana.
6. The Respondent No. 4, Haryana Renewable Energy Development Agency
("HAREDA") is an agency of the Government of Haryana functioning as the
nodal agency for implementation of various renewable energy schemes and
projects in the State. The Respondent No. 5, Sh. Sahab Singh, is private
Respondent residing at Village Harewa, Tehsil Chhachhroli who had moved an
application before the Haryana Commission for being impleaded as a necessary
party to defend his interest and those of affected farmers of nearby villages. The
Page 3 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
Haryana Commission impleaded him as a necessary party by order dated
07.01.2015.
Facts of the case
7. On 07.06.1999, a tripartite Memorandum of Understanding (“MoU”) was
executed between HAREDA, the Irrigation Department, Government of Haryana,
and the Appellant ( BPCL) for development of a 4 MW Small Hydro Project at
Dadupur, Western Yamuna Canal (Lower). Subsequent to MoU, in 2002, BPCL
prepared and submitted the Detailed Project Report ( “DPR”) for setting up of 6
MW of small hydro project at the site and it was approved by HAREDA on
18.04.2003.
8. On 27.12.2006, the HPGCL submitted the PPA, for approval of State
Commission. The State Commission, vide its Order dated 10.07.2007, approved
the PPA and approved the Tariff for the project based on Project cost of Rs
3259.52 lakhs as per DPR of 2006. The tariff was determined at Rs.2.80 per
unit for the first 12 years and Rs.1.70 per unit for years 13 to 15, from the date of
commissioning. On 03.03.2008 Appellant and UHBVN signed the PPA.
9. The Project was commissioned on 19.03.2010. It is the case of Appellant
that after commissioning of the Project, FSL of 916 ft. could not be maintained
on account of seepage and waterlogging affecting adjoining agricultural land and
crops. Consequently, the pond level was maintained at a lower level. The issue
was considered by the Irrigation Department and other concerned authorities and
various measures were examined for addressing the seepage problem.
Page 4 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
10. Prior to commissioning, on 17.03.2010, the Appellant had approached the
Commission seeking re-determination of tariff on account of increase in the
Project cost and additional works undertaken for the Project. The Commission,
vide Order dated 08.09.2010, revised the project tariff to Rs.3.18 per unit for the
first 12 years and Rs.1.93 per unit for the 13th to 15th years. The said Order was
challenged before this Tribunal in Appeal No.78 of 2011, however this Tribunal
vide its order dated 27.04.2012 disposed of the Appeal No. 78 of 2011 and inter
alia, held that the original tariff had not been determined under Section 63 of the
Electricity Act, 2003 and that the Commission was empowered under Section 62
of the Act and the applicable Regulations to re-determine the tariff.
11. The Appellant represented to the Irrigation Department and HAREDA that
the Project had been designed on the basis of an FSL of 916 ft. and that operation
at a lower FSL was resulting in substantial reduction in generation. However
same could not be resolved.
12. Appellant then filed Case No. HERC/PRO-59 of 2014 before the
Commission seeking re-determination of tariff applicable to the Project on the
basis of the realistic FSL available at Dadupur Pond and consequential revision
of tariff from the date of commissioning. The State Commission, vide the
Impugned Order dated 18.12.2015, dismissed the said petition. Aggrieved by the
aforesaid Order, the Appellant has preferred the present Appeal.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF APPELLANT
13. The issue in the present case arises from the Irrigation Department’s
inability to maintain the pondage at the FSL of 916 ft., which, as per Clause 8 of
the MoU, was the Government’s undertaking to enable sustainable power
Page 5 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
generation and was not an independent obligation of BPCL. Tariff determinations
were premised on the availability of the said FSL, as the DPR’s estimated annual
generation of 31.5 MU formed the basis of the tariff approved in 2007, while the
additional capital cost approved in 2010 was intended to enable BPCL to
“maintain a PLF/CUF of 56%”. Further, HAREDA and the Respondent No.3
repeatedly affirmed FSL of 916 ft. as the agreed project parameter in their
subsequent correspondence, including BPCL’s letter dated 15.12.2010 and the
joint inspection culminating in the Irrigation Department’s letter dated 16.03.2011.
However, at the review meeting dated 24.07.2013, the Engineer-in-Chief,
Irrigation Department, while acknowledging that “the Dadupur Pond has been
designed for FSL of 916 ft.”, stated that “FSL at 916 ft. cannot be allowed”,
whereupon the Appellant requested that this position be communicated in writing
to enable it to approach HERC. It was this refusal, and not any default on the part
of the Appellant, that led to the filing of Petition on 17.11.2014 before the
commission and, thereafter, the present Appeal.
14. It is further submitted that the shortfall in generation is not attributable to
any obligation or deficiency on the part of BPCL, but is a direct consequence of
the Government’s refusal to honour its undertaking under Clause 8 of the MoU.
The Appellant’s own reciprocal obligation under Clause 21 was confined to
making alternate arrangements for uninterrupted water flow and strengthening
the banks in the vicinity of the Project, an obligation it exceeded by constructing,
at its own cost, a new gated regulator and renovating the Additional Head
Regulator gates, expressly to enable it “to maintain the required F.S.L. pond level
of 916.0 ft.”. Further, WAPCOS’s report, commissioned by the Irrigation
Department, traced seepage predominantly to causes “essentially unrelated to
the Canal”, while acknowledging that canal seepage falls within the State’s
domain; thus, no deficiency on the Appellant’s part is established on record.
Page 6 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
Further, the only risk undertaken by the Appellant under Clause 19 of the MoU
was that of seasonal variations in hydrological data and discharge patterns, i.e.,
variations in the quantum of water flowing through the canal from season to
season, which cannot be construed as an assumption of risk arising from a
reduction in FSL or storage level, a structural parameter of the pond within the
Irrigation Department’s control and conceptually distinct from seasonal discharge
variations. It is submitted that ‘Head’, as identified in the Notice, is the difference
between the Head Race Level and the Tail Race Level, and power generation
varies directly with Head and Discharge; consequently, when the Irrigation
Department fails to maintain pondage at the FSL, the Head Race Level falls,
resulting in a corresponding reduction in Head and generation below the
designed capacity. This direct physical relationship is illustrated by the fact that
HPGCL, operating on the same canal with a greater Head, achieves
correspondingly higher generation capacity. Since the tariff was determined on
the presumption that pondage would be maintained up to the FSL of 916 ft., its
non-maintenance necessitates redetermination of the tariff on the basis of the
realistic storage level actually available, namely, 912–913 ft.
15. HERC’s order dated 10.07.2007 expressly stipulated that the tariff would
“continue to be in force till such time it is reviewed and approved by the
Commission”, thereby envisaging its review and redetermination. The revisable
nature of the tariff under Section 62, the requirement to determine the final tariff
on the basis of the actual cost of the completed project, and HERC’s power to
review the tariff during the tariff period were affirmed by this Tribunal in UHBVNL
v. HERC, Appeal No. 78 of 2011, decided on 27.04.2012. A conjoint reading of
the PPA and the two tariff orders establishes that the tariff was fixed for a period
of 15 years and must be considered in light of the project parameters on which it
was determined.
Page 7 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
16. It is further submitted that the finding in the Impugned Order that the Project
was “ill-conceived” is contrary to the material on record. The project parameters,
including the site, Head, Discharge and FSL, were determined and repeatedly
reaffirmed by the Government’s own instrumentalities, beginning with the
Haryana State Electricity Board’s scheme in the mid-1970s and the Central
Electricity Authority’s clearance dated 16.11.1981, followed by the Chief
Engineer’s approval of the FSL of 916 ft. on 20.11.2006. Significantly, the
Impugned Order itself records that, as early as 2003, the Technical Evaluation
Committee had noted that the existing head regulator gate could attain only 914.8
ft., as against the “maximum designed pond level” of 916 ft., and had
recommended remodelling “for attaining a head of 916 ft.…”, thus, the deficiency
in the Government’s infrastructure was known to the authorities before approval
of the DPR and execution of the PPA and cannot be attributed to the Appellant.
17. This Tribunal, in Greenyana Solar (P) Ltd. v. HERC, Appeal No. 302 of
2024, decided on 23.04.2025 (paras 15–16), held that project-specific tariff
redetermination under Section 62 is tailored to the economic and operational
realities of the project and reflects the actual costs incurred, subject to prudence
check. Further, in Patikari Power Ltd. v. HPERC, APTEL Appeal No. 179 of
2010, decided on 23.04.2012 (paras 36 and 45(ii)), this Tribunal redetermined
the tariff where the hydrology provided by the State’s own entities fell short of the
envisaged parameters, holding that such circumstances amounted to a change
in the basic parameters, dependent on natural conditions and beyond the
appellant’s control. The present case stands on an equal, if not stronger, footing,
as the FSL of 916 ft. was represented and envisaged by the Government’s own
instrumentalities, but was subsequently not maintained by them, resulting in a
change in the basic project parameters beyond the Appellant’s control.
Page 8 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
Accordingly, the Appeal deserves to be allowed and the tariff redetermined on the
basis of the realistic FSL and storage level actually available at Dadupur Pond,
in accordance with Regulation 29 of the HERC RE Tariff Regulations, 2010, and
the principles laid down in Greenyana Solar and Patikari Power.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF RESPONDENT NO.2 (HPPC)
18. It is submitted that the dispute concerning the maintenance of the FSL is
essentially inter se the Appellant and Respondent No. 3 (Irrigation Department),
as any assurance regarding the FSL arises, if at all, from the MoU dated
07.06.1999, to which Respondent No.2 is not a party. The PPA dated 03.03.2008
neither stipulates any FSL requirement nor imposes any obligation upon
Respondent No.2 in respect of the pond level. Further, the Force Majeure clause
(Clause 6.1) does not cover inadequate FSL, and no notice under Clause 6.1(b)
was issued by the Appellant. Moreover, Clause 2(ii) of the PPA expressly
absolves Respondent No.2 of any expenditure incidental to the remodeling of
existing structures. Accordingly, the consequences of a dispute between the
Appellant and Respondent No. 3 cannot be imposed upon HPPC or passed on
to the consumers of Haryana by way of tariff redetermination.
19. It is submitted that, under Clauses 3, 5, 8, 19 and 21 of the MoU, the
Appellant was responsible for conducting further investigations, assessing
hydrological data and project feasibility, and strengthening the canal banks and
related structures at its own cost. The DPR also mandated thorough site
investigation. Despite the Project capacity being increased from 4 MW to 6 MW,
the Appellant failed to adequately assess the feasibility of maintaining the FSL at
916 ft. The Impugned Order records that the DPR underwent revisions in 2006–
07 without examining the FSL and site suitability for the 6 MW Project, that the
Page 9 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
Appellant proceeded on the assumption of an FSL of 916 ft. without adequate
financial prudence or risk assessment, that the causes subsequently identified by
WAPCOS ought to have been ascertained at the inception stage, and that the
Appellant’s failure to strengthen the banks aggravated seepage. Respondent No.
3 and HAREDA consistently raised these objections, whereas the Appellant
offered only a general denial. The correspondence further demonstrates that the
Appellant was aware of the issue, proposed remedial measures of its own, and
that Respondent No. 3 relied upon its assessment; however, the measures
proved inadequate, and the WAPCOS-recommended measures were not
undertaken due to “apprehensions”. Significantly, all such correspondence was
exchanged with Respondent No. 3 and HAREDA, and Respondent No.2 was
never informed of the issue. The Appellant did not dispute the WAPCOS findings,
except with regard to the cost and time involved. Moreover, the remedies
recommended by WAPCOS, namely canal lining costing Rs 33.51 crore and an
X-regulator costing Rs 5.25 crore, pertain to canal works falling within the domain
of the Appellant and Respondent No. 3, and not the purchaser. The Impugned
Order considers all relevant clauses, correspondence and the conduct of the
parties, is well reasoned, and calls for no interference.
20. It is submitted that the issue of FSL was never raised by the Appellant in its
first petition dated 17.03.2010, and the order dated 08.09.2010, which also
recorded the Appellant’s failure to survey and reassess the additional work
required, was never challenged by it. Despite the availability of full-year
generation data for FY 2010–11 (12.93 MUs), the Appellant raised no such issue
before any forum, except through correspondence with Respondent No. 3 and
HAREDA , and even accepted an interim FSL of 912.8–913.4 ft. The Appellant
had already benefited from tariff redetermination on the basis of the completed
project cost, whereby the tariff was enhanced from Rs 2.80 to Rs 3.18 per unit, a
Page 10 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
determination upheld by this Tribunal as being based on actual cost, while HERC
allowed approximately Rs 4 crore out of the claimed Rs 8.25 crore for reasons
duly recorded. The subsequent filing of Petition No. 59 of 2014 on 17.11.2014 is
therefore an afterthought. Having accepted and acted upon the order dated
08.09.2010, which attained finality and was upheld in Appeal No. 78 of 2011, the
Appellant is estopped from reopening the issue, which is also barred by the
principle of res judicata, as recognised in GUVNL v. GERC, Appeal No. 279 of
2013, decided on 22.08.2014
21. It is contended that the present case is squarely covered by Puri Oil Mills
Ltd. v. HPPC, Appeal No. 90 of 2013, decided on 09.04.2014 (J-1), wherein this
Tribunal, in similar circumstances involving a canal-based project, held that
strengthening the canal banks was the developer’s responsibility, that adequate
time was available for due diligence, and that there was no valid ground to reopen
the PPA or award compensation for loss of generation. Further, the Hon’ble
Supreme Court, in HPPC v. Sasan Power Ltd., 2023 SC 42, decided on
06.04.2023 held that a bidder who fails to verify the relevant position “acted at his
own peril” and that a Commission “cannot rewrite a contract solemnly entered
into” or exercise regulatory powers contrary to its express terms. The sanctity of
the PPA and the impermissibility of altering the agreed tariff to the prejudice of
consumers have likewise been affirmed in GUVNL v. Solar Semiconductor
Power Co., CA No. 6399 of 2016, decided on 25.10.2017; GUVNL v. EMCO
Ltd., (2016) 11 SCC 182; and TRANSCO v. Sai Renewable Power, (2011) 11
SCC 34, para 86. The Appellant’s reliance on GUVNL v. Tarini Infrastructure,
(2016) 8 SCC 743, is distinguishable, as that case involved a factual mistake
regarding the evacuation point, which increased the distance from 4 km to 23 km
and resulted in an unforeseen expenditure of Rs 10 crore. No comparable
Page 11 of 30

Judgement in Appeal No. 55 of 2016
supervening event exists in the present case, and a defect inherent at the
inception of the Project cannot be treated as a Force Majeure event.

40. In hydroelectric projects, the Full Supply Level (FSL) denotes the maximum
water level in the reservoir under normal operating conditions, corresponding to
100% of its designed storage capacity. It represents the highest elevation to
which water is stored for routine purposes such as power generation, irrigation,
and municipal supply, but excludes flood situations. While the correlation
between Head, Discharge, and generation is undeniable, the responsibility to
revalidate the declared FSL and design the project accordingly rests squarely
with the developer. In our considered view, it is incumbent upon the project
developer, as proponent of the hydroelectric scheme, to undertake
comprehensive and independent studies to cross-verify the Full Supply Level
(FSL) indicated and to determine parameters like design head, design discharge,
and consequently the installed capacity and tariff viability of the station. It is
noteworthy that the project was initially conceived as a 4 MW installation.
However, upon completion of detailed studies and investigations, the Appellant
itself proposed enhancement of the capacity to 6 MW, with a projected design
energy of 31.5 MUs and a Plant Load Factor of 59.95%.
41. Prudence requires that the developer validate the declared FSL through
hydrological yield analysis, topographical and geological surveys, sedimentation
and silt yield studies, and environmental and social impact assessments, so that
the reservoir level is not overstated beyond what is realistically attainable. The
ratio of UHBVNL judgement does apply in the present issue, as the Appellant is

52. We are also of the view that since the principal issue in the Petition before
the State Commission, as well as in the present Appeal pertained to revision of
tariff on account of non-availability of FSL, being beyond the control of Appellant,
and Appellant wished to rely upon these documents to buttress its case,
permission ought to have been sought to place these documents on record before
this Tribunal during the hearing itself. This would have afforded the Respondent
an opportunity to rebut any claim based on such documents and to contest the
reasons for their non-production before the Commission.
53. A general query from the bench does not entitle the Appellant to place on
record documents, after the matter has been reserved for judgement, particularly
when such documents pertain to a period prior to passing of impugned order. The

54. Nevertheless, in the interest of justice, we have examined the documents

they have been assured a tariff based on design parameters of the project so
finalised by the Appellant. As such, the issue of non-achievement of FSL of 916
ft. is not an inter se matter between the Appellant and the Respondent-Discom.
The Respondent-Discom, and consequently the consumers, cannot be saddled
with the burden of enhanced tariff on this account.
55. It is reiterated that, had the Appellant exercised proper due diligence and
accurately estimated the project parameters including cost, design energy, and
financial viability, such matters could and ought to have been conclusively
determined at the DPR stage itself, prior to execution of the PPA. Instead, the
Appellant has sought piecemeal enhancement in tariff, firstly on account
increases in cost, and now reduction in design energy thereby attempting to shift
the burden of its own lapses onto the Respondent-Discom and ultimately the
consumers. Proper investigation and validation of project parameters is the sine
